questions.q: Roughly what is the radius of an atom?
questions.explain: An atom has a radius of about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The nucleus is far smaller, roughly 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m, around ten thousand times smaller than the atom.

questions.q: What are isotopes?
options: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of protons
Charged atoms that have lost electrons
questions.explain: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons) but with different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers.

questions.q: What did the alpha particle scattering experiment lead Rutherford to conclude?
options: Atoms are a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded in it
Mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus
Electrons orbit at fixed distances in shells
questions.explain: Most alpha particles passed straight through but a few were deflected back, showing the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus — replacing the plum pudding model.

questions.q: What is the activity of a radioactive source?
options: The rate at which its nuclei decay, measured in becquerel (Bq)
The number of undecayed nuclei remaining
The energy of each emitted particle
questions.explain: Activity is the rate at which nuclei of a source decay, measured in becquerel (Bq), where 1 Bq is one decay per second.

questions.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most strongly ionising but the least penetrating?
questions.explain: Alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising but least penetrating — it is stopped by a sheet of paper or a few cm of air.

questions.q: A nucleus undergoes alpha decay. How do its mass number and atomic number change?
options: Mass number stays the same, atomic number +1
questions.explain: An alpha particle is ⁴₂He, so the nucleus loses 4 from its mass number and 2 from its atomic number.

questions.q: What is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
options: The time for the source to completely decay
The time for the number of undecayed nuclei to halve
The time for the activity to double
Half the age of the sample
questions.explain: Half-life is the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei in a sample to halve (equivalently for its activity/count-rate to halve).

questions.q: What is the difference between irradiation and contamination?
options: Irradiation means a radioactive material gets onto or into an object; contamination means being exposed to radiation from a source
Irradiation means being exposed to radiation from a source; contamination means having radioactive atoms on or inside an object
They are exactly the same thing
Contamination only happens with gamma radiation
questions.explain: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an external source (the object does not become radioactive). Contamination is when radioactive atoms get onto or inside an object, which then continues to emit radiation.

questions.q: What is nuclear fusion?
options: A large unstable nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei
Two light nuclei joining to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
A nucleus emitting an alpha particle
questions.explain: Fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy (as in the Sun). Fission is the splitting of a large unstable nucleus into smaller ones.

questions.q: Which particles are found inside the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explain: The nucleus contains protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral). Electrons (negative) orbit the nucleus in energy levels (shells).

questions.q: The nuclear notation for an atom is ¹⁴₆C. How many neutrons does it contain?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 14 − 6 = 8. The atomic number 6 gives the number of protons.

questions.q: Which scientist provided evidence for the existence of the neutron?
questions.explain: James Chadwick's experiments (about 20 years after the nuclear model) provided evidence for the neutron. Bohr proposed electron energy levels; Thomson devised the plum pudding model.

questions.q: Radioactive decay is described as a random process. What does this mean?
options: The source decays at a steady, predictable rate per nucleus
It is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when
Decay only happens when the source is disturbed
All nuclei decay at exactly the same time
questions.explain: Decay is random: you cannot predict which nucleus will decay or when. A Geiger–Müller tube can measure the overall count-rate, but individual decays are unpredictable.

questions.q: Which material is needed to absorb (significantly reduce) gamma radiation?
options: Thick lead or several metres of concrete
questions.explain: Gamma is the most penetrating: paper stops alpha, a few mm of aluminium stops beta, but gamma needs thick lead or metres of concrete to reduce it significantly.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits a beta-minus particle, how does its atomic number change?
questions.explain: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton (plus the emitted electron), so the mass number is unchanged but the atomic number increases by 1.

questions.q: A source has an activity of 800 Bq. Its half-life is 6 hours. What is its activity after 18 hours?
questions.explain: 18 hours = 3 half-lives. Activity halves each time: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 Bq.

questions.q: An atom is electrically neutral. This is because it has an equal number of...
options: neutrons and protons in the nucleus only
questions.explain: Atoms are neutral because they contain equal numbers of positive protons and negative electrons, so the charges cancel.

questions.q: In the nuclear symbol of an atom, what does the bottom (smaller) number represent?
questions.explain: The bottom number is the atomic (proton) number — the number of protons. The top number is the mass number (protons + neutrons).

questions.q: What was Bohr's key contribution to the development of the atomic model?
options: He suggested electrons orbit the nucleus at specific fixed distances (energy levels)
He proposed the plum pudding model
He fired alpha particles at gold foil
questions.explain: Bohr adapted the nuclear model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances (energy levels), which matched experimental observations.

questions.q: What is a beta (β⁻) particle?
options: A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus
A proton ejected from the nucleus
questions.explain: A beta-minus particle is a high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton. An alpha particle is a helium nucleus; gamma is an EM wave.

questions.q: In the alpha decay ²³⁸₉₂U → X + ⁴₂He, what is the mass number and atomic number of nucleus X?
questions.explain: Mass and charge are conserved: mass 238 − 4 = 234 and atomic number 92 − 2 = 90, giving X = ²³⁴₉₀Th.

questions.q: The count-rate from a source falls from 240 counts/min to 30 counts/min. If the half-life is 30 minutes, how much time has passed?
questions.explain: 240 → 120 → 60 → 30 is 3 halvings, so 3 half-lives have passed: 3 × 30 = 90 minutes.
